content: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD), also known by its Latin binomial Aphthae epizooticae, is an extremely contagious and sometimes fatal viral disease that primarily affects cattle and pigs. It can also infect other cloven-hoofed animals such as deer, goats, and sheep, as well as non-cloven-hoofed animals like elephants, rats, and hedgehogs. Human infections are exceedingly rare. The causative agent of FMD is the foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV), which is the prototype member of the Aphthovirus genus within the Picornaviridae family. This virus is responsible for an acute systemic vesicular disease that affects cattle and other animals globally. FMDV is highly variable and transmissible. The viral nature of FMD was first identified in 1897 by Friedrich Loeffler. He demonstrated this by passing the blood of an infected animal through a fine porcelain filter, which removed bacteria, and found that the filtered fluid could still transmit the disease to healthy animals. When FMDV comes into contact with a host cell, it binds to a receptor site on the cell surface, triggering the folding-in of the cell membrane. Once inside the host cell, the virus's protein coat dissolves, allowing the viral RNA and protein components to be synthesized in large quantities. These components are then assembled into new viral particles. After assembly, the host cell lyses (bursts), releasing the newly formed viruses to infect other cells. FMD is caused by FMDV, a member of the Aphthovirus genus in the Picornaviridae family. Viruses in this family are small (25–30 nm), non-enveloped, icosahedral particles containing single-stranded RNA as their genetic material. There are seven serotypes of FMDV: O, A, C, SAT-1, SAT-2, SAT-3, and Asia-1. These serotypes exhibit some regional specificity, with the O serotype being the most prevalent worldwide. FMD occurs in many regions across the globe. While some countries have successfully eradicated the disease, its wide host range and rapid transmission make it a significant concern for international animal health. The incubation period for FMD typically ranges from 3 to 8 days. The disease is characterized by a high fever that subsides after two to three days, followed by the appearance of blisters in the mouth, which lead to excessive secretion of stringy or foamy saliva and drooling. Blisters also form on the feet, which may rupture and cause lameness. Adult animals often experience weight loss, which can take several months to recover. In mature males, swelling of the testicles may occur, while in cows, milk production can decline significantly.
